position: attributive only — *the actual cost*; not *the cost was actual*
form: -al from *act*; the adverb *actually* means на самом деле
contrast: Not *актуальный*. *actual* = real, the one that exists or happened, as opposed to what was planned, expected or imagined (действительный, фактический). For *актуальный* say *relevant*, *current*, *timely* or *pressing*: *актуальная тема* = *a timely (relevant) topic*, *актуальная информация* = *up-to-date information*, *это уже не актуально* = *that's no longer relevant*. The adverb *actually* is на самом деле, вообще-то — never актуально. *In actual fact* sounds British and formal; Americans say *in fact* or *actually*. *actual* goes only before a noun.

senses.gloss: Real; existing or happening in fact, as opposed to what was planned, expected or imagined.
examples: The *actual* cost of the repairs was almost twice the estimate.
Is that based on an *actual* study, or did you just read it online?
The movie is loosely based on *actual* events.

senses.gloss: The thing itself — the exact or main one, as opposed to what comes before it or around it.
examples: The reception lasted all night, but the *actual* ceremony took twenty minutes.
Those were his *actual* words — I'm not making this up.
We drove around for an hour before we found the *actual* entrance.

position: both — the nervous-system sense is attributive only: *the sympathetic nervous system*
takes: *to* or *toward* + a person or their trouble (понимающий); *to* or *toward* + an idea or cause (поддерживающий); *about* + a problem
contrast: Not *симпатичный*. *sympathetic* = understanding and kind about someone's problems (сочувствующий, отзывчивый), or in favor of an idea. *He's very sympathetic* does not mean he is good-looking or nice to be around. For *симпатичный* say *cute*, *attractive* or *good-looking* (о внешности) and *nice* or *likable* (о человеке). What follows *to* changes the meaning: *sympathetic to her* (сочувствует ей) but *sympathetic to the plan* (одобряет план). In a movie or novel, *a sympathetic character* is one the audience likes and cares about — the one place where it comes close to симпатичный.

senses.gloss: Showing that you understand and care about someone's problems or pain.
examples: My boss was really *sympathetic* when my dad got sick.
She gave me a *sympathetic* smile.
The nurses couldn't have been *more sympathetic*.

senses.gloss: Agreeing with or supporting an idea, a group or a cause.
examples: Several senators are *sympathetic* to the proposal.
The judge seemed *sympathetic* toward the union's side.

senses.gloss: Of a character in a story, movie or show: easy to like, so that you care what happens to them.
examples: The writers made the villain surprisingly *sympathetic*.
It's hard to write a *sympathetic* hero who lies to everyone.

senses.gloss: In medicine: relating to the part of the nervous system that gets the body ready for action.
examples: Stress switches on the *sympathetic* nervous system.
The drug blocks *sympathetic* nerve signals to the heart.

form: from Latin *accuratus* 'done with care' — English kept 'exact', Russian kept 'neat'
contrast: Not *аккуратный*. *accurate* = correct and exact, without mistakes (точный, верный). For *аккуратный* say *neat* or *tidy* (о вещах, почерке, внешности) and *careful* (о работе и человеке): *аккуратный почерк* = *neat handwriting*, *аккуратный водитель* = *a careful driver*, *он очень аккуратный* = *he's very neat*. *She's very accurate* would mean her answers or her aim are exact, not that she keeps things tidy. The noun is *accuracy* (точность).

senses.gloss: Correct and true in every detail; free from mistakes.
examples: Is this map still *accurate*?
The article gives an *accurate* picture of life in a small town.
The new tests are much *more accurate* than the old ones.

senses.gloss: Able to hit a target or to measure something exactly.
examples: He's the *most accurate* passer in the league.
My kitchen scale isn't very *accurate*.
You need an *accurate* throw to get the runner out at first.

position: both — the 'dressed' sense is predicative only: *Are you decent?*
takes: *of* + person + *to*-infinitive (*decent of you to call*); *to* + person (*He's been decent to me*)
contrast: *decent* is praise with a limit. *The food was decent* means неплохая, вполне нормальная — acceptable, not excellent; for отличная say *great* or *excellent*. *A decent salary* is one you can live on, not a big one. Said of a person, *decent* is порядочный — honest and kind — not *достойный* in the sense of 'distinguished'. The opposite *indecent* is only непристойный: a mediocre meal is not *indecent*. Do not mix up *decent* (DEE-suhnt) with the noun *descent* (dih-SENT, спуск, происхождение).

senses.gloss: Good enough; of an acceptable or fairly good quality, size or amount.
examples: Is there a *decent* coffee shop around here?
He makes a *decent* living as a plumber.
The seats were pretty *decent* for the price.

senses.gloss: Honest, fair and kind; morally good.
examples: Her father is a *decent*, hardworking man.
It was *decent* of you to drive me all the way home.
He's the *most decent* guy I've ever worked for.

senses.gloss: Proper and socially acceptable; not likely to shock or offend.
examples: He was told to wear something *decent* to court.
Wait until a *decent* hour to call them — don't wake them up at six.

senses.gloss: Informal: dressed enough to be seen by other people.
examples: Can I come in? Are you *decent*?
Give me a minute — I'm not *decent* yet.

contrast: Not *интеллигентный*. *intelligent* = smart, quick to learn and understand (умный). It says nothing about manners, education or culture — a rude, uneducated person can be very *intelligent*. For *интеллигентный* say *cultured*, *well-educated*, *refined* or *well-mannered*; *интеллигенция* is *the intelligentsia* or *educated people*. *intellectual* is someone who lives by ideas and books (интеллектуал). In everyday American speech *smart* is more common than *intelligent*.

senses.gloss: Good at learning, understanding and thinking; clever.
examples: She's one of the *most intelligent* students I've ever taught.
Dolphins are highly *intelligent* animals.
He's *intelligent* but lazy.

senses.gloss: Of a question, choice or remark: showing good thinking or judgment.
examples: That's a very *intelligent* question.
Selling the house before prices dropped was an *intelligent* move.

senses.gloss: Able to think and understand, as humans can.
examples: Are we the only *intelligent* species in the universe?
Scientists are still looking for signs of *intelligent* life in space.

senses.gloss: Of a machine or system: using a computer to react to conditions and make simple decisions on its own.
examples: The car has an *intelligent* braking system that stops it before a crash.
*Intelligent* thermostats learn when you're usually home.

takes: *It is sensible* + *to*-infinitive; *of* + person + *to*-infinitive (*sensible of you to wait*)
contrast: *sensible* is not *sensitive*. *sensible* = reasonable and practical, showing good sense (разумный, благоразумный); *чувствительный* is *sensitive*: *sensitive skin*, *a sensitive child*. *He's very sensible* means he makes wise, practical choices, not that he is easily hurt. The nouns split the same way: *sense* (здравый смысл) goes with *sensible*, *sensitivity* with *sensitive*; *sensibility* is taste and feeling (*an artistic sensibility*). In old or very formal writing, *sensible of* means *aware of* (*sensible of the honor*); do not use it in everyday English.

senses.gloss: Showing good judgment; reasonable and practical.
examples: Wearing a helmet is the *sensible* thing to do.
She's a *sensible* kid — she won't do anything stupid.
It would be *more sensible* to wait until spring.

senses.gloss: Of clothes and shoes: practical and comfortable rather than fashionable.
examples: Wear *sensible* shoes — we'll be walking all day.
She traded her heels for a pair of *sensible* flats.

takes: *for* + person (*ambitious for her son*) or thing (*ambitious for power*); *to*-infinitive (*ambitious to succeed*)
contrast: Russian *амбициозный* often sounds negative — proud, touchy, full of oneself — and *с амбициями* can mean vain. English *ambitious* is usually positive or neutral: it means wanting to achieve a lot (целеустремлённый). For the negative Russian sense say *arrogant*, *conceited*, *full of himself* or *self-important*. *An ambitious plan* is about size, not vanity — it is big and hard to carry out; *too ambitious* or *overly ambitious* means it probably can't be done.

senses.gloss: Having a strong wish to succeed, to become important, or to get rich or powerful.
examples: She's smart and *ambitious*, and she wants to run her own company someday.
*Ambitious* young lawyers often work eighty hours a week.
His parents are very *ambitious* for him.

senses.gloss: Of a plan, goal or project: large and needing a lot of effort, money or skill to succeed.
examples: The city has an *ambitious* plan to plant a million trees.
Finishing the whole house in a month was probably too *ambitious*.
This is the band's *most ambitious* album yet.

contrast: Not *патетический* and not *пафосный*. *pathetic* = pitiful (жалкий), and in everyday American speech it is usually an insult: *That's pathetic!* = Жалкое зрелище! Позорище! For *патетический* (passionate, lofty, solemn) say *impassioned*, *passionate* or *solemn*: *патетическая речь* = *an impassioned speech*. For *пафосный* (showy, pretentious) say *pompous*, *pretentious* or *over the top*. Calling a speech *pathetic* says it was terrible, not emotional.

senses.gloss: Informal: so bad, weak or useless that it makes you feel contempt or annoyance.
examples: That's the *most pathetic* excuse I've ever heard.
Our defense was *pathetic* last night.
Only three people showed up? That's *pathetic*.

senses.gloss: Making you feel pity or sadness.
examples: The *pathetic* little puppy was shaking in the rain.
There was something *pathetic* about the old man eating alone every night.

position: both — the theater sense is attributive only: *dramatic arts*
contrast: Russian *драматический* and *драматичный* often mean tragic or full of suffering. English *dramatic* most often means sudden and big — *a dramatic change* (резкое, разительное изменение), *a dramatic improvement* — and the change can be a good one. For *драматическая ситуация* say *a tragic*, *dire* or *desperate situation*. *Don't be so dramatic* = Не устраивай драму, не преувеличивай. *драматический театр* is simply *a theater*.

senses.gloss: Of a change or event: sudden, large and very noticeable.
examples: There's been a *dramatic* drop in crime downtown.
The new coach made a *dramatic* difference.
The rise in rents has been *more dramatic* here than anywhere else in the state.

senses.gloss: Exciting and impressive to watch or look at.
examples: The movie ends with a *dramatic* rescue at sea.
The house has *dramatic* views of the canyon.

senses.gloss: Of a person or behavior: showing feelings in an exaggerated way, to get attention.
examples: Stop being so *dramatic* — it's just a scratch.
She made a *dramatic* exit, slamming the door behind her.

senses.gloss: Relating to plays, acting or the theater.
examples: He studied *dramatic* arts in college.
The festival includes *dramatic* readings of new plays.

contrast: Russian *конкретный* is much wider than *concrete*. Use *concrete* with *evidence*, *proof*, *plans*, *proposals*, *steps*, *examples* and *results* — things that are definite instead of vague. For one particular thing or person say *specific* or *particular*: *конкретная дата* = *a specific date*, *конкретный человек* = *a particular person*, *в конкретном случае* = *in this particular case*, *конкретно* = *specifically*. Slang *конкретный* ('real, serious') has no match in *concrete*. In *a concrete wall* (бетонная стена) the word is the noun *concrete* used as a modifier, not this adjective.

senses.gloss: Based on facts, clearly stated and definite; not vague or general.
examples: The police have no *concrete* evidence against him.
Our plans for the summer aren't *concrete* yet.
Could you give me a *more concrete* example?

senses.gloss: Existing as a real thing that can be seen and touched; not abstract.
examples: Young children learn math faster with *concrete* objects like blocks.
A *concrete* noun names something you can see or touch, like a chair or a dog.

contrast: Not *деликатный* about a person. *a delicate person* is physically weak or easily hurt (хрупкий, болезненный), not tactful. For *деликатный человек* say *tactful*, *considerate* or *discreet*: *он очень деликатный* = *he's very tactful*. The words overlap only for situations: *a delicate matter* = деликатный, щекотливый вопрос. *деликатес* is the noun *a delicacy*.

senses.gloss: Easily broken or damaged; needing careful handling.
examples: Wash *delicate* fabrics by hand.
Babies have very *delicate* skin.
These old photos are too *delicate* to touch.

senses.gloss: Of a person or their health: weak and likely to get sick.
examples: She was a *delicate* child who missed a lot of school.
Grandpa's health is *delicate*, so we keep our visits short.

senses.gloss: Of a situation or subject: needing tact and care, because it could easily cause trouble or hurt feelings.
examples: Money is a *delicate* subject in our family.
The peace talks are at a *delicate* stage.
This is going to need a *more delicate* approach.

senses.gloss: Small, fine and graceful.
examples: She has *delicate* features and dark eyes.
The earrings hang from a *delicate* gold chain.

senses.gloss: Of a taste, smell or color: light and pleasant, not strong.
examples: This fish has a *delicate* flavor, so go easy on the sauce.
The bedroom is painted a *delicate* shade of blue.

senses.gloss: Of work or an instrument: needing great skill and precision, or precise enough to notice very small changes.
examples: Removing the tumor was a *delicate* operation.
These *delicate* instruments can detect the smallest movement.

contrast: It has nothing to do with *спектакль*, which is *a play*, *a show* or *a performance*. *spectacular* = amazing, stunning, very impressive to see (потрясающий, зрелищный). *The play was spectacular* means it was wonderful, not that it was theatrical. *A spectacular failure* is a huge, very public one. As a noun, *a spectacular* is a big, showy TV or stage show.

senses.gloss: Very impressive and exciting to see; stunning.
examples: The view from the top of the trail is *spectacular*.
This year's Fourth of July fireworks were *more spectacular* than ever.
She scored a *spectacular* goal from midfield.

senses.gloss: Unusually great in size or degree, often suddenly so.
examples: The company's first year was a *spectacular* success.
His run for mayor ended in *spectacular* failure.
The town has seen *spectacular* growth since the factory opened.

position: attributive only — *prospective buyers*; not *the buyers are prospective*
contrast: Not *перспективный*. *prospective* = likely to become something or to happen in the future (будущий, потенциальный): *a prospective student* is someone thinking of applying, not a promising one. For *перспективный* say *promising*, *up-and-coming* or *with a future*: *перспективный молодой игрок* = *a promising young player*, *перспективное направление* = *a promising field*. Do not confuse it with the noun *perspective* (точка зрения; перспектива в рисунке).

senses.gloss: Likely or expected to become a particular kind of person in the future.
examples: The realtor is showing the house to *prospective* buyers this weekend.
*Prospective* students can tour the campus on Fridays.
She met her *prospective* in-laws for the first time at Thanksgiving.

senses.gloss: Expected or likely to happen; relating to the future.
examples: The report looks at the *prospective* costs of a new stadium.
Researchers ran a *prospective* study that followed 5,000 patients for ten years.

contrast: Not *гениальный*. *genial* = friendly and cheerful (добродушный, приветливый), and it describes people and their manner, not ideas. For *гениальный* say *brilliant* or *ingenious*: *гениальная идея* = *a brilliant idea*, *гениальный изобретатель* = *a brilliant (ingenious) inventor*; informally, *That's genius!* *A genial idea* is not English. The first syllable is JEE, not GEN.

senses.gloss: Friendly, cheerful and pleasant to be with.
examples: Our *genial* host made sure everyone had a drink.
He has a *genial* smile and a firm handshake.
Her husband is *more genial* than she is, and everyone likes him.

senses.gloss: Literary: of weather or a climate, pleasantly mild and warm.
examples: They moved to Arizona for its *genial* climate.
The *genial* spring sun brought everyone out to the park.

type: classifying; also quality (*a very artistic child*)
position: both — the 'relating to art' sense is attributive only: *artistic director*
contrast: Russian *артистичный* and *артистический* come from *артист* — a performer or actor. English *artistic* comes from *artist* — above all a painter, sculptor or other creative person — and means good at art or creative. For *артистичный* say *theatrical*, *a natural performer* or *has stage presence*; *артистическая уборная* is *a dressing room*. Informal *artsy* (American) is often mocking: *an artsy coffee shop*.

senses.gloss: Relating to art or artists.
examples: The director was given complete *artistic* freedom.
The painting has more *artistic* value than market value.

senses.gloss: Of a person: naturally good at art, or creative in other ways.
examples: Both of her kids are very *artistic* — they're always drawing.
I'm not *artistic* at all; I can't even draw a straight line.
He's *more artistic* than his brother, who's into math.

senses.gloss: Made or arranged with skill and good taste; attractive.
examples: The cake had an *artistic* design of sugar flowers.
The chef arranges every plate in an *artistic* way.

form: -ed adjective, pronounced /ɪd/; there is no everyday verb *sophisticate*
contrast: It is not about *софистика* (sophistry — clever but dishonest arguing), and it is not simply *complicated*. *sophisticated* is usually praise: of a person, worldly and cultured (искушённый, утончённый); of technology, advanced and well designed (сложный, современный). *sophisticated software* is advanced; *complicated software* is hard to use. For the negative *изощрённый* (*изощрённая жестокость*) say *elaborate* or *calculated*, not *sophisticated*. The noun *a sophisticate* means a sophisticated person.

senses.gloss: Of a person, place or style: knowing a lot about the world, culture and fashion; elegant.
examples: She was the *most sophisticated* woman in our small town.
The restaurant has a *sophisticated*, grown-up feel.
Four years in New York made him a lot *more sophisticated*.

senses.gloss: Of a machine, system or method: advanced and complex.
examples: The bank uses *sophisticated* software to spot fraud.
Today's phones are far *more sophisticated* than the computers that went to the moon.

senses.gloss: Of a person's thinking or an audience: able to understand difficult ideas; not simple or naive.
examples: Voters are more *sophisticated* than politicians think.
The novel offers a *sophisticated* look at race and class.

takes: *with* + money or time (*extravagant with money*); *in* + praise or claims (*extravagant in their praise*)
contrast: Not *экстравагантный* in its usual Russian sense — eccentric, unusual, outlandish. English *extravagant* is mainly about money and excess: *an extravagant gift* costs too much, *an extravagant person* spends too much (расточительный). For *экстравагантный* say *eccentric*, *flamboyant*, *outlandish* or *unconventional*: *экстравагантный наряд* = *a flamboyant (outlandish) outfit*, *экстравагантный человек* = *an eccentric*. The two words meet only in sense 3, where a party or costume is both costly and showy.

senses.gloss: Spending much more money than is wise, or costing much more than is wise.
examples: They live an *extravagant* lifestyle on a teacher's salary.
A new car is an *extravagant* birthday present for a sixteen-year-old.
He was never *extravagant* with money.

senses.gloss: Of claims, praise or promises: far more than is reasonable or true.
examples: Be careful of *extravagant* claims about weight-loss pills.
The critics were *extravagant* in their praise.

senses.gloss: Very elaborate and showy.
examples: It was the *most extravagant* wedding I've ever been to.
She wore an *extravagant* hat covered in feathers.

position: both — the insurance sense is attributive only: *comprehensive coverage*
form: -ive from *comprehend* in its old sense 'take in, include'
contrast: Not *comprehensible* (понятный). *comprehensive* = complete, covering everything (всеобъемлющий, исчерпывающий): *a comprehensive report* is long and thorough, not easy to understand. Russian *комплексный* is often *comprehensive* in English — *комплексный подход* = *a comprehensive approach*, *комплексное обследование* = *a comprehensive checkup* — and not *complex*, which means сложный. In American car insurance, *comprehensive coverage* pays for damage that does not come from a collision: theft, hail, a falling tree.

senses.gloss: Including all or almost all the facts, parts or details; complete and thorough.
examples: The list of trails on the website isn't *comprehensive*, but it covers the popular ones.
Graduate students take *comprehensive* exams at the end of their second year.
It's the *most comprehensive* guide to the city I've seen.

senses.gloss: Of insurance: covering most kinds of loss; in American car insurance, covering damage not caused by a collision.
examples: My *comprehensive* coverage paid for the hail damage on the car.
If the car is stolen, you'll only get paid if you have *comprehensive* insurance.

position: both — the technical sense is attributive only: *complex numbers*
contrast: Not *комплексный*. *complex* = made of many parts and hard to understand (сложный). For *комплексный* say *comprehensive*, *integrated* or *combined*: *комплексный подход* = *a comprehensive approach*, *комплексные меры* = *a package of measures*, *комплексный обед* = *a lunch special*. Only in math is *complex number* = комплексное число. As a noun, *a complex* is a group of buildings (*a sports complex*) or a psychological problem (*an inferiority complex*); *у него комплексы* is more naturally *he's insecure* or *he has hang-ups*. *complex* and *complicated* are close: *complicated* is more everyday and suggests confusion; *complex* is more neutral and formal. Never *complexer*.

senses.gloss: Made of many connected parts, and so difficult to understand or deal with.
examples: Climate change is a *complex* problem with no easy answer.
The tax code gets *more complex* every year.
The human brain is the *most complex* thing we know of.

senses.gloss: In science, math and grammar: made of two or more parts joined together, as in *complex numbers* or *complex sentences*.
examples: Whole grains are full of *complex* carbohydrates.
A *complex* sentence has a main clause and at least one dependent clause.

position: attributive only — *the eventual winner*; not *the winner was eventual*
contrast: Not *эвентуальный* (possible, in case something happens). *eventual* = final, coming at the end of a long process: *the eventual winner* is the one who won in the end. For *эвентуальный* or *возможный* say *possible* or *potential*: *эвентуальные риски* = *possible risks*. The adverb has the same trap: *eventually* = в конце концов, в итоге — never возможно (*possibly*).

senses.gloss: Happening or existing at the end of a process or a period of time.
examples: The Giants, the *eventual* champions, lost their first three games.
The *eventual* cost of the bridge was three times the original budget.
Doctors hope the drug will lead to an *eventual* cure.
